title: Cong Wei (@CongWei1230)
summary:
Diffusion Self-Guidance for Controllable Image Generation
paper page:
introduce self-guidance, a method that provides greater control over generated images by guiding the internal representations of diffusion models. We demonstrate that properties such as the shape, location, and appearance of objects can be extracted from these representations and used to steer sampling. Self-guidance works similarly to classifier guidance, but uses signals present in the pretrained model itself, requiring no additional models or training. We show how a simple set of properties can be composed to perform challenging image manipulations, such as modifying the position or size of objects, merging the appearance of objects in one image with the layout of another, composing objects from many images into one, and more. We also show that self-guidance can be used to edit real images.

title: Cong Wei (@CongWei1230)
summary:
ConsistI2V
Enhancing Visual Consistency for Image-to-Video Generation
paper page:
Image-to-video (I2V) generation aims to use the initial frame (alongside a text prompt) to create a video sequence. A grand challenge in I2V generation is to maintain visual consistency throughout the video: existing methods often struggle to preserve the integrity of the subject, background, and style from the first frame, as well as ensure a fluid and logical progression within the video narrative. To mitigate these issues, we propose ConsistI2V, a diffusion-based method to enhance visual consistency for I2V generation. Specifically, we introduce (1) spatiotemporal attention over the first frame to maintain spatial and motion consistency, (2) noise initialization from the low-frequency band of the first frame to enhance layout consistency. These two approaches enable ConsistI2V to generate highly consistent videos. We also extend the proposed approaches to show their potential to improve consistency in auto-regressive long video generation and camera motion control. To verify the effectiveness of our method, we propose I2V-Bench, a comprehensive evaluation benchmark for I2V generation. Our automatic and human evaluation results demonstrate the superiority of ConsistI2V over existing methods.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GFx9BvEXUAANovJ.jpg

Snap Video
Scaled Spatiotemporal Transformers for Text-to-Video Synthesis
Contemporary models for generating images show remarkable quality and versatility. Swayed by these advantages, the research community repurposes them to generate videos. Since video content is highly redundant, we argue that naively bringing advances of image models to the video generation domain reduces motion fidelity, visual quality and impairs scalability. In this work, we build Snap Video, a video-first model that systematically addresses these challenges. To do that, we first extend the EDM framework to take into account spatially and temporally redundant pixels and naturally support video generation. Second, we show that a U-Net - a workhorse behind image generation - scales poorly when generating videos, requiring significant computational overhead. Hence, we propose a new transformer-based architecture that trains 3.31 times faster than U-Nets (and is ~4.5 faster at inference). This allows us to efficiently train a text-to-video model with billions of parameters for the first time, reach state-of-the-art results on a number of benchmarks, and generate videos with substantially higher quality, temporal consistency, and motion complexity. The user studies showed that our model was favored by a large margin over the most recent methods.

title: Cong Wei (@CongWei1230)
summary:
💭Reinforcement Learning (RL) is making waves everywhere, however, the development of code generation models is still driven by pure SFT without any RL. What’s the real roadblock? Our answer is the lack of reliable reward signals.
🔥We’re excited to introduce 🂡 AceCoder, a new approach that trains RM and performs RL (both rm-based and rule-based) through large-scale coding datasets (89K) with an average of 16 automatically generated test cases per question.
What does this unlock? Massive improvements across the board:
🚀 Best-of-N sampling: +10 pts for Llama-3.1-8B-Ins, +5 pts for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Ins—bringing a 7B model on par with DeepSeek-V2.5 (236B)!
🚀 RL tuning: Boosts Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct beyond GPT-4-Turbo on MBPP.
🚀 Direct RL from a base model: +25% on HumanEval-plus, +6% on MBPP-plus—achieved in just 80 steps (48 GPU hours)!
These results show that RL for code has massive untapped potential—with scalable reward models and automated test generation, we’re only getting started!
We released all the models and datasets we have curated and hope to set a new standard to push the limit of the code generation model.

title: Cong Wei (@CongWei1230)
summary:
Introducing QuickVideo, 🚀 speeding up the end-to-end time from the mp4 bit stream to VideoLLM inference by at least 2.5 times for hour-long video understanding (e.g 1024 frames) on a single 40GB GPU.
🤔What are the key challenges of hour-long video understanding?
1. Surprisingly long time (up to minutes) to decode thousands of frames directly from the mp4 bit stream, yet this is ignored by almost all previous works.
2. High memory bottleneck! Up to more than 100GB of activation memory from attention and MLP layers (even with flash attention) and more than 300GB KV cache memory for one million visual tokens from 1 hour video. (Analysis based on InternVL 2.5-8B)
3. The inherent high computation cost due to the quadratic nature of the attention mechanism.
🤩In QuickVideo, we solve it by:
1. ⚡QuickCodec: A brand-new video decoding library that decodes video blocks concurrently instead of sequentially with 2-3× speedup and exactly the same decoded frames.
2. 🧠QuickPrefill: A group-based video context prefilling strategy that reduces activation memory to less than 1GB and achieves 50% KV cache memory and computation reduction while preserving more than 97% accuracy on 4 long video understanding benchmarks!
3. ⚙️QuickVideo: Conducts video decoding and prefilling group by group in an interleaving way to avoid idle time of either CPU or GPU, reducing end-to-end time from 70 seconds to 20 seconds for a 30-minute video example on a single 40GB GPU!

Introducing VerlTool - a unified and easy-to-extend tool agent training framework based on verl.
Recently, there's been a growing trend toward training tool agents with reinforcement learning algorithms like GRPO and PPO. Representative works include SearchR1, ToRL, ReTool, and ToolRL. While these achieve impressive performance, their training codes are either not fully open-sourced or too difficult to modify and customize with new tools, creating unexpectedly high engineering costs for the community when exploring new ideas.
To address these issues and reduce engineering overhead, we propose verl-tool.
Key Features:
1. 🔧 Complete decoupling of actor rollout and environment interaction - We use verl as a submodule to benefit from ongoing verl repo updates. All tool calling is integrated via a unified API, allowing you to easily add new tools by simply adding a Python file and testing independently.
2. 🌍 Tool-as-environment paradigm - Each tool interaction can modify the environment state. We store and reload environment states for each trajectory. For each training, you can launch
3. ⚡ Native RL framework for tool-calling agents - verl-tool natively supports multi-turn interactive loops between agents and their tool environments.
4. 📊 User-friendly evaluation suite - Launch your trained model with OpenAI API alongside the tool server. Simply send questions and get final outputs with all interactions handled internally.
We've successfully reproduced ToRL results using our verl-tool framework, demonstrating its correctness and demonstrating comparable performance on mathematical benchmarks.
VerlTool is an active ongoing project! We aim to incorporate more tools covering a wide range of use cases and expect they can be trained together in a single framework. Suggestions and contributions are highly welcomed!

I have been thinking a lot about what retrieval should look like when agents become stronger at planning, coding, and tool use. Classic RAG and retrieval agents expose a corpus through a top-k retriever: efficient, scalable, and extremely useful — but also a compressed interface. The agent only sees what the retriever decides to surface.
A simple analogy: top-k retrieval is like asking a librarian to bring you a small cart of likely relevant books. DCI is closer to an open-stack research library, where the agent can enter the corpus, search exact phrases, inspect nearby context, follow weak clues, and verify hypotheses locally.
For humans, walking through the library would be painfully slow. For agents and computers, grep, file reads, and small scripts make this kind of direct interaction cheap, composable, and surprisingly effective.
This is the core question we wanted to study:
As foundation models become stronger, is top-k retrieval still the best interface for search — or is it becoming a bottleneck?
📈 The results are surprisingly strong.
On BrowseComp-Plus, with the same Claude Sonnet 4.6 backbone:
🔎 Qwen3-Embedding-8B retriever: 69.0% accuracy, $1,440
🧰 DCI-Agent-CC: 80.0% accuracy, $1,016
That is +11.0 accuracy points while reducing cost by 29.4%.
DCI also generalizes beyond deep research, reaching 83.0 avg accuracy on multi-hop QA and 68.5 avg NDCG@10 on IR ranking — without relying on conventional sparse/dense retrieval pipelines.
🧩 The most interesting finding is why DCI works.
DCI does not simply win by retrieving more gold documents. In many cases, retrieval agents already surface useful evidence, but fail to convert it into the next reasoning step.
It helps because it gives the agent higher retrieval interface resolution. Once the agent reaches a promising document, it can localize, inspect, compose, and verify evidence at a much finer granularity.
The gain is less about “more recall” and more about turning weak evidence into actionable evidence.
That said, DCI is not a free lunch.
Our ablations show a clear operating envelope: DCI is powerful once it finds a useful anchor document, but as the corpus grows, finding that first anchor becomes more expensive. In short, DCI scales well in search depth, but not automatically in search breadth.
The tool-set and context-management results point to the same lesson. A simple read + grep interface already captures much of the gain, while open bash improves accuracy further at higher cost. And for long-horizon search, the best context strategy is not to keep the most text, but to preserve the right working state.
So the takeaway is not: “Replace every retriever with grep.” The stronger point is that retrieval for agents should become an interface-design problem, not only a retriever-design problem.
I believe future retrieval agents will be hybrid and adaptive: semantic retrieval to find anchors, DCI-style interaction to inspect and verify evidence, and context management to keep long searches stable.
The question is no longer only:
“Which embedding model gives the best top-k?”
It is also:
“What operations should an agent have over knowledge?”
DCI is our first step toward this direction: treating retrieval as a high-resolution interaction layer between agents and corpora.

🚀 Introducing Function-Aware FIM Mid-Training — turning ordinary code into internet-scale training signal for coding agents!
Everyone scales synthetic agent trajectories in post-training. We look one stage earlier: the base model is never optimized for the conditioning structure that agentic training demands.
💡 Key insight: a coding agent step (action → observation → continuation) is structurally isomorphic to a function call site (call → return → downstream usage). Ordinary code already contains agent-shaped supervision — at internet scale, for free.
Our recipe: mask whole functions selected via program dependency graph analysis + a complexity–inferability criterion, embed CoT rationales inside the FIM middle, and run it as a dedicated mid-training stage before agentic post-training.

✅ SWE-Bench-Verified +2.8 / +3.0 / +3.2 on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/14B & Qwen3-8B; Lite up to +5.4

summary:
In this Gemini Notebook video overview, we are going to take a look at :
PixelUMM is an encoder free unified multimodal model created by NVIDIA and the University of Waterloo that handles both visual understanding and generation directly in pixel space without relying on traditional pretrained visual encoders or variational autoencoders.
The work was done by :
Cong Wei1,2 Xuanchi Ren1 Bryan Chu1 Weiming Ren2 Huan Ling1 Jiahui Huang1
Laura Leal-Taixé1 Sanja Fidler1 Wenhu Chen2 Zian Wang1 Jay Zhangjie Wu1
By representing images as spatial patches and videos as spatiotemporal tubelets connected to a Mixture of Transformers backbone via single layer linear projections, the framework jointly supports autoregressive text prediction and pixel space flow matching. The system utilizes generalized causal attention and a structured training schedule to process diverse tasks, including image and video understanding alongside text to image and text-to-video generation. Empirical analyses examine key design choices such as patch size and decoder alternatives, showing that less aggressive spatial and temporal compression improves performance while maintaining competitive results across multiple benchmarks.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTrAMEgbsAAd-ef.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2106207089483993088/vid/avc1/480x270/4CiUc0C5o89IABTr.mp4?tag=29
clean_summary:
Usually, models that understand or generate images and videos rely on pretrained visual encoders or autoencoders to process visual data. This adds complexity and can limit flexibility. PixelUMM, created by NVIDIA and the University of Waterloo, skips these steps by working directly with pixels, treating images as spatial patches and videos as spatiotemporal tubelets.

PixelUMM connects these patches and tubelets to a Mixture of Transformers backbone using simple linear projections. It supports tasks like text prediction, image and video understanding, and text-to-image or text-to-video generation. By using generalized causal attention and a structured training schedule, it balances spatial and temporal compression to improve performance while staying competitive on benchmarks.
